title: Robots and the Future of Work
intro: You should spend about 20 minutes on this passage.

paras.t: Few subjects raise stronger feelings than the effect of robots on employment. Some people fear that machines will take every job within a generation, while others believe that technology has always created more work than it has destroyed. Both sides can point to history. In the early nineteenth century, English textile workers known as Luddites smashed the new looms that threatened their livelihoods, yet within a few decades there were more jobs in the textile industry than ever before, although they were different jobs, in different places, for different workers.

What is different now, according to the economist Dr Peter Lindgren, is the range of tasks that machines can perform. The machines of the industrial revolution replaced muscle. Modern software and robots can also recognise speech, read medical scans and write simple reports, tasks that were once thought to need a human mind. A widely quoted study from Oxford University in 2013 estimated that almost half of the jobs in the United States could be automated within twenty years, although many experts regard that figure as too high.

A more careful approach is to look at tasks rather than whole jobs. Very few occupations consist entirely of routine activities that a machine could do; most contain a mixture of routine tasks and tasks that need judgement, creativity or care for other people. On this analysis, estimates suggest that only about one job in ten is at high risk of being automated, though roughly one in three is likely to change significantly. A bank clerk may spend less time counting money, but more time advising customers.

The kind of work most at risk is the routine, repetitive kind: assembling parts, sorting parcels, processing forms. Those who do such work are often the least well paid and the least able to retrain. Jobs that are hardest to automate include those that need dexterity in unpredictable surroundings, such as plumbing or nursing, and those that depend on emotions, such as teaching and therapy. Ironically, some highly paid professional work, such as analysing legal documents, may be easier for a machine than cleaning an office.

Governments and companies are therefore considering how to help workers through the change. Some propose a universal basic income, a regular payment to every citizen whether or not they work. Supporters say it would provide security and make it easier for people to retrain; opponents say it would be very expensive and might discourage work. Others prefer to invest in education, so that workers can move to new kinds of jobs. Experiments have been carried out in Finland and in several other countries, but their results are still being debated.

There is a further argument that the benefits of automation depend on how they are shared. If machines make firms richer but leave workers poorer, the effect on society could be harmful, however efficient the factories may be. Professor Aiko Matsuda points out that the shorter working week, introduced in many countries in the twentieth century, was the result of political choices as well as of new machines. In her view, the question is not what technology will do to us, but what we choose to do with it.

In the end, nobody can be sure what the working world will look like in thirty years. Past predictions about technology have often been wrong, in both directions: flying cars have not arrived, but few people in 1990 foresaw how much of their lives would be spent with a telephone that has the power of a computer. The sensible response is perhaps to prepare in several ways at once: to teach flexible skills, to support those who lose their jobs, and to keep watching the evidence, instead of relying on fear or on hope.
